title: Detection of Exploits
summary: This strategy detects the staging and testing of exploits against your environment, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1587.004 (Develop Capabilities: Exploits). Before a campaign, an adversary builds or buys an exploit and tests it somewhere, and the testing often touches systems that can see it: internet facing decoy services, canary tokens, exposed application endpoints, and crash reporting pipelines. Detection therefore uses honeypot interaction logs, request pattern analysis in web and application logs, and process crash telemetry, because a crafted request that lands correctly very often produces an unexpected crash or error before it succeeds. The important correlation is repetition of an identical, unusual request across multiple targets within a short period, which distinguishes deliberate testing from a single user error. The limit of this strategy is that successful exploitation can be silent, so crash and decoy evidence catches the failures and the probing but not every attempt.

beginner.definition: An exploit is a piece of input that abuses a weakness in software. Attackers build and test exploits before using them. This detection looks for the testing, using decoy systems, unusual repeated requests, and software crash records. It gives you a warning before the real attack.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers test quietly against small targets first. One crash is usually nothing, but the same strange request hitting many machines in minutes is a test. Crash records are valuable because they exist even when the attack fails. Early warning lets you patch or isolate the affected software before it is used against you for real.
howItWorks: Decoy services on your network record every connection and payload they receive.
Web and application logs show requests, including ones with unusual lengths, encodings, or repeated parameters.
Crash and error reporting tools record when a service stops unexpectedly and what it was doing.
The detection groups identical or near identical requests across many targets in a short window.
Real payloads sent to a decoy service raise the score immediately.
The analyst confirms the affected product and version, then patches or restricts access.
beginner.example: Think of a shop that leaves one empty till on the counter. Nobody is meant to use it, so any receipt printed on it is interesting. If the same person tries the same broken card on that till and on three other tills within a minute, the manager knows someone is testing the payment system. The empty till is a decoy, and the receipts are the evidence.
takeaways: Failed exploitation leaves traces in crash and error records, so those logs carry real value.
Repeating the same unusual request across many targets is the strongest sign of testing.
Decoy services give you high confidence alerts and almost no false positives.

objectives: Explain how adversaries build and test exploits before using them in an operation
Identify decoy, application, and crash telemetry that reveal exploit testing
Recognise request patterns that indicate crafted input rather than ordinary user error
Correlate crash evidence with request logs to identify the targeted product and version
Prioritise patching and mitigation using evidence from test activity
dataSources: Honeypot and decoy service logs recording source address, destination port, and full request payload
Web server and application logs with request length, parameters, encoding, and response status codes
Crash and error reporting from endpoint or application monitoring tools including faulting module and version
Intrusion detection and prevention alerts for exploit signatures with source, destination, and signature name
File integrity or application monitoring events showing unexpected service restart or configuration change after a crash
logic: The detection looks for two related patterns. The first is interaction with a service that should receive no traffic at all, such as a decoy endpoint, which is high confidence evidence of deliberate probing and testing. The second is the same unusual request, identified by a stable hash of method, path template, and parameter structure, arriving at several hosts within a short window, together with a crash or unexpected restart of the same service component shortly afterwards. Fields that must be correlated are the source address, the request fingerprint, the targeted host and application version, the crash signature, and the timing between the request and the fault. The benign version is a monitoring probe or a broken client that repeats one malformed request against one host, or a scheduled security scan from an approved range. The malicious version spreads across hosts, varies the payload to defeat simple matching, and produces repeated faults in one binary on the same day.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Repeated Anomalous Request Pattern With Matching Service Crash
# logsource:
#   product: web
#   category: webserver
# detection:
#   selection:
#     http.request.method|in: [GET, POST]
#   anomaly:
#     http.request.body.length: > 2000
#     http.response.status_code|in: [500, 400, 403]
#   crash:
#     event.type: application_crash
#     process.name|endswith: .so
#   filter_scanners:
#     source.ip|in: approved_scanner_ranges
#   condition: (selection and anomaly | count() by source.ip > 15 within 5m) or crash and not filter_scanners
# level: high
falsePositives: Application security testing and fuzzing performed by your own teams against staging systems
Legacy clients or scripts that send a malformed request in a retry loop and cause repeated errors
Faulty application releases that crash under normal load and generate the same responses for all users
Approved vulnerability scanners that probe deep parameter sets and occasionally trigger error conditions
Content delivery or load balancer health checks that send unusual headers and receive error responses by design
tuningNotes: Scope the decoy service branch to honeypots only and keep it at a high severity with no filters, because the false positive rate is close to zero. For the request branch, require the same request fingerprint on at least five distinct hosts inside five minutes, add approved scanner ranges and health check user agents to the filter, and exclude hosts that are already in a degraded state due to a known incident. Record the faulting module and version from crash reports so the alert names the product. The coverage you lose by requiring multiple hosts is a single target exploitation attempt, which needs host based exploit detection and patch monitoring to cover; keep a daily report of unique anomalous request fingerprints for manual review.
